rv.q: “Is This a Room,” which opened on Monday at the Lyceum Theater, turns the ums and stutters and bizarre non sequiturs of recorded speech into astonishing — and astonishingly emotional — theater.
In Tina Satter’s eerie, essential play about the NSA-leaker Reality Winner, the nature of everything seems to waver.
Ms. Loomer has turned what might have been a dry-as-dust documentary drama into a taut, compelling piece of theater.
The production succeeds in making Winner's interrogation feel immediate and visceral, transforming a sterile government transcript into something approaching high drama.
It's a confession as close to illuminating the human condition as any.
It’s a fascinating piece in every way, replete with fabulous central performances from both Emily Davis (who plays Winner) and Pete Simpson (who plays the lead FBI agent at the interrogation).
The verbatim transcript becomes a gripping psychological thriller in the hands of director Tina Satter and star Emily Davis.

Tina Satter's highly absorbing A Room is based on the verbatim transcript of the FBI's initial interview.
It’s an unsettling feeling, and indeed “A Room” is an unsettling play, which Broadway could certainly use more of.
The note-perfect production simply leaves no space for extraneous imaginings.
The play just sort of starts and ends, without fanfare or adornment, and yet, in its heightened presentation of reality, emerges as one of the most radical works on Broadway.
For already making that unsettling Trump administration accomplishment perfectly clear, Satter deserves many thanks.
Thankfully, for now, she can (sort of) speak for herself in Is This a Room.
"At 70 minutes, A Room begs for context, and that post-theater flier isn’t enough.
Doesn’t that sound a lot better than sitting through a show that is both mediocre and long?
Her play is not about the reality of Reality Winner but the surreality of modern existence, so much of which keeps us in the dark.
Is This a Room feels like a breath of fresh air in the commercial theater realm.
It’s a visionary work that will certainly help put documentary theater back on the map, while also making us question what is even real.
But I think by not telling the whole story, “A Room” is almost as guilty as Winner of letting the American people down.

cn.t: Critics praise this verbatim FBI transcript as a surprisingly gripping psychological thriller, with Tina Satter's direction transforming 65 minutes of documentary material into taut, anxiety-inducing drama led by Emily Davis's compelling performance.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
